title: Mass replace from the command line
summary: Preview with rg -r, edit with sed, perl or PowerShell, feed file lists through xargs, survive GNU versus macOS sed and PowerShell quoting, and review it all with git diff.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: replacing across a repository
steps.body: When a rename touches 300 files, nobody clicks through them. These are the commands people chain together, always on a clean Git tree, always previewed first and reviewed after.

toolkit.what: Preview a replacement. rg prints every matching line as it would look after the replace, and never edits a file. Its replacement syntax is $1, ${name}, $0.
flags: show the replacement in the output (files are not changed)
with -l: end each file name with NUL, for xargs -0
toolkit.when: before every mass replace, to see exactly what will change

toolkit.what: Stream editor: rewrite files in place. With -E, groups and + ? | work without backslashes; \1 is a group and & the whole match. GNU sed knows \b and \w, but not \d (use [0-9]).
flags: BSD (macOS): edit in place, no backup; the '' is required
after the last /: every match on a line, not just the first
toolkit.when: Linux boxes, containers and CI runners

toolkit.what: Perl edits in place with a full PCRE-style engine: \d, lookarounds, lazy quantifiers, named groups. It behaves the same on Linux and macOS.
flags: loop over every line and print it
edit in place (-i.bak keeps a backup)
the program comes next on the command line
read the whole file at once, for multi-line patterns
toolkit.when: you need lookarounds or \d, or one command that works on every Unix

toolkit.what: Find the files with rg, then hand the list to the editor. Only files that contain a hit are rewritten, so timestamps and line endings elsewhere stay untouched.
flags: read NUL-separated names, so spaces in paths survive
the same list, but only files Git tracks
toolkit.when: the rename spans the whole repository

toolkit.what: PowerShell's -replace uses .NET regex and .NET replacement syntax. The brackets read the whole file before Set-Content writes it.
flags: case-sensitive replace (what you want for code)
read the file as one string, not an array of lines
single quotes, so PowerShell leaves $1 alone
do not add an extra line break at the end

toolkit.what: Review what the replace really did before anything is committed. If it is wrong, throw it away and try again.
flags: files and line counts: did it touch files it should not?
stage hunk by hunk, skipping the bad ones
toolkit.when: after every mass replace, before the commit

steps.prompt: Match each command or flag to what it does.
pairs: extended regex: groups and `+ ? |` without backslashes
print the result of the replace without changing any file
pass file names safely, even with spaces in them
edit in place with lookarounds, `\d` and lazy quantifiers

steps.prompt: Complete the command: rewrite every C# file that calls `GetUser(`, with names that may contain spaces.
steps.explain: `xargs -0` turns the NUL-separated list from `rg -l -0` into arguments for `sed`, and `sed -i` edits each file in place. On macOS it would be `sed -i ''`.

items: See what the rename would produce before touching anything
Show a reviewer the new lines in a PR comment without editing files
An in-place edit in an Ubuntu CI runner
An in-place edit on your MacBook with the built-in sed
The replacement needs a lookahead and `\d`
One script that must behave the same on Linux and macOS
steps.explain: `sed -i.bak` also works on both systems, but Perl gives you the same engine everywhere, with the features ERE lacks.

steps.title: Preview: .Result to await
prompt: Blocking on `task.Result` in async code risks deadlocks and starves the thread pool. You want to preview,
with `rg -r`, what replacing every `name.Result` with `await name` would look like. rg uses `$1` like .NET.
Write the pattern and replacement: `var user = userTask.Result;` becomes `var user = await userTask;`.
Properties that only start with `Result`, like `Results` or `ResultCode`, must not change.
hints: Capture the identifier before `.Result`, and end with `\b` so `Results` does not match.
Pattern `(\w+)\.Result\b`, replacement `await $1`. On the command line: `rg '(\w+)\.Result\b' -r 'await $1' -g '*.cs'`.
steps.explain: This is exactly why you preview: the output shows the lines to fix, and also the ones a regex should not touch (`GetUser(id).Result` is not matched because of the `)`; it needs a hand edit). Each method that gains an `await` must become `async`, which the compiler will point out.

steps.title: PowerShell: single quotes, and case
body: PowerShell's `-replace` is .NET's `Regex.Replace`, so `$1`, `${name}` and `$0` work. Two rules make or break it:
**1. Single quotes around the replacement.** In double quotes PowerShell expands variables **before** `-replace`
runs. `$1` is an (empty) PowerShell variable, so `"$3-$2-$1"` arrives as `--`.
If you also need a PowerShell variable in it, join the pieces: `'$1-' + $suffix`.
**2. `-replace` and `-match` ignore case by default.** `'ID id Id' -replace 'id','Key'` changes all three.
For code, use `-creplace` and `-cmatch`, the case-sensitive versions.

steps.explain: In double quotes, PowerShell expands `$2` and `$1` to empty strings before the regex runs, so each version becomes a lone `-`. With single quotes it prints `9-1 10-1`. `-creplace` only changes the lower-case `id`.

steps.prompt: The same script works in CI on Ubuntu, but on your Mac it fails like this. Why?
options: macOS (BSD) sed requires an argument after `-i`: it took the script as the backup suffix and then read `app.config` as the script. Use `sed -i '' ...`, or `-i.bak`, which works on both.
macOS sed does not support the `g` flag.
The file has Windows line endings, which BSD sed cannot read.
steps.explain: On BSD sed, `-i` always takes a suffix (it may be empty: `''`). The error names the file because sed is trying to run `app.config` as a command: `a` is sed's append command. `brew install gnu-sed` gives you GNU sed as `gsed` if you prefer one syntax everywhere.

steps.title: Symptom: the build broke after a rename
prompt: **Symptom.** A teammate ran `sed -E -i 's/GetUser/GetUserAsync/g'` over the repository. The build now fails:
```text
error CS0103: The name 'GetUserAsyncName' does not exist in the current context
error CS0117: 'UserRepository' does not contain a definition for 'TryGetUserAsync'
`git diff` also shows `GetUserAsyncAsync(` where the script ran twice. Fix the pattern and replacement (shown
here in .NET syntax) so only calls to the method `GetUser` itself are renamed, and a second run changes nothing.
hints: Require the opening bracket right after the name, and a word boundary before it.
steps.explain: The `\(` stops `GetUserName` and `GetUserAsync` from matching, so the replace is idempotent, and `\b` keeps `TryGetUser` out. In sed it is `s/\bGetUser\(/GetUserAsync(/g`. The lesson behind the symptom: preview with `rg -r`, then read `git diff --stat` before you commit.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a safe mass rename in order.
lines: git status                                  # start from a clean tree
git diff --stat && git diff                 # review what changed
also: git status                                  # start from a clean tree
git diff --stat && git diff                 # review what changed
steps.explain: A clean tree means `git restore .` can undo the whole replace in one go. Preview first, review after, and let the compiler and the tests have the last word.

steps.title: A replace that takes its text from config
prompt: A support tool rewrites canned replies: each rule from the config says "replace the word X with Y". Write
`string ReplaceWord(string text, string word, string with)` that replaces every **whole-word** occurrence
of `word` with `with`.
Both come from the config, so treat both as plain text:
- `word` may contain regex characters (`v1.2`): escape it.
- `with` may contain `$` (prices!). A replacement string is a language too: `$0.99` would insert the match.
Escape every `$` as `$$`, or return `with` from a lambda, which is never interpreted.
| text | word | with | result |
| `Price: FREE today` | `FREE` | `$0.99` | `Price: $0.99 today` |
| `use v1.2 not v1x2` | `v1.2` | `v1.3` | `use v1.3 not v1x2` |
`System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
starter: string ReplaceWord(string text, string word, string with)
solution: string ReplaceWord(string text, string word, string with)
template: Dojo.Eq("a price with $ is inserted as written", "Price: $0.99 today", ReplaceWord("Price: FREE today", "FREE", "$0.99"));
Dojo.Eq("the dot in v1.2 is literal", "use v1.3 not v1x2", ReplaceWord("use v1.2 not v1x2", "v1.2", "v1.3"));
Dojo.Eq("only whole words: FREEDOM stays", "FREEDOM is $0.99", ReplaceWord("FREEDOM is FREE", "FREE", "$0.99"));
Dojo.Eq("$$ in the config stays $$", "Total: $$5", ReplaceWord("Total: AMOUNT", "AMOUNT", "$$5"));
hints: Pass `with.Replace("$", "$$")` as the replacement, or use `m => with`.
